chunks.text: 有一个让人不太舒服的事实要接受：在谷歌上搜索你餐厅名字出来的第一条结果，很可能根本不是你的网站。而是从右边滑出来的那块侧边栏面板——营业时间、电话、那五张小得不行的照片、二〇一九年那条一星半的差评、二〇二一年有人不小心加上去的那个"已永久关闭"的小标签。那块面板就是你的谷歌商家资料，对大多数独立餐厅来说，你网站以为自己在做的活儿，有百分之八十其实是它在做。
我自己经营两家餐厅，还给另外几十家做网站。每当有新客户预约打电话来，我打开的第一个标签页不是他们的首页，而是他们的谷歌商家资料。我想看他们碰过哪些字段、选了哪些分类、上一次发照片是什么时候、是在认真回复评价还是装作评价不存在。百分之九十的情况下，我在三十秒内就能看出他们为什么把街客流量输给了隔壁街区那家。几乎从来不是因为菜不好。
这篇文章就是我在那通电话里会过一遍的清单——按照我实际过的顺序，带上那些没人告诉你、直到谷歌复审把你逮住你才会知道的具体设置。

这是谷歌在打量一家餐厅资料时看到的东西。左边，一份不完整的资料：只有名字、地址和电话。也许还有一张店面模糊的照片。开业日期空着。属性空着。菜单链接指向一个 P D F。三年前留下两条评价，都没有回复。右边，一份完整的资料：具体的主分类、十条附加属性、一段提到街区和招牌菜的简介、一个指向真正 H T M L 页面的菜单链接、一个预订链接、每周更新的谷歌动态、二十张近期照片、百分之九十五的评价回复率。同一家餐厅。在本地地图包里的排名天差地别。这两张卡片之间的差距，就是周二被人找到和找不到之间的差距。
建好一份资料大概要半个小时。真正把它优化好，再加一个小时。大多数老板做完第一部分就停了，跳过第二部分——这就是为什么左边那张卡片比右边常见得多。下面我来讲怎么把两部分都做完。
第一步——认领或创建你的商家资料。
谷歌可能已经根据公开数据为你的餐厅建好一份资料了。在谷歌地图里搜你的餐厅名字。如果出现了，点"认领此商家"或者"您是这家商家的所有者吗？"然后按提示走。如果没出现，就从零开始建一份：
打开 business.google.com
点击"立即管理"或"添加您的商家"
填入你餐厅的准确法定名称——招牌上挂的那个名字，不是塞满关键词的那种。"The Irish Inn at Glen Echo"是对的。"The Irish Inn — Best Irish Pub Restaurant Glen Echo MD"就不对了，谷歌可能会因此暂停你的资料。
选择你的业务分类。先选"餐厅"，然后再加一个更具体的主分类（见下面第三步）。
填入地址。如果你是实体餐厅，填实体地址。不要勾选"我为客户在他们的所在位置提供商品和服务"，除非你真的用自己的员工做配送。
加上电话号码和网站 U R L。
第二步——验证所有权。
Google needs to confirm you actually own or manage this restaurant. The most common verification methods in twenty twenty-six:

Video verification. This is now the default method for most new listings. Google asks you to record a short video showing your storefront, signage, and interior. Upload it through the G B P app or dashboard. Approval typically takes a few days.
Phone call or text. Available for some businesses. Google calls or texts the number on file with a verification code.
Email. Sometimes available if Google can confirm your domain ownership.

Postcard by mail. Google used to send a postcard with a PIN to your address (5–14 days). This method has been largely phased out in favor of video verification but may still appear as an option in some cases.
Do not skip verification. An unverified listing cannot respond to reviews, post updates, or access analytics — and it ranks worse than a verified one.

Video verification sounds like the fastest option on paper and then your approval sits pending for eleven days and you are about to open a new patio. My honest tip: if you are ever offered postcard-by-mail as a fallback, take it. Slower on average, but it has an actual bounded timer — you know within two weeks if it worked. Video verification can ghost you for a month and you have no recourse but to re-record and re-upload.

Also: record the video on the same phone you will use to manage the listing afterward . Google's systems correlate device fingerprints. Switching devices mid-process triggers a manual review that adds days.
Step 3 — Choose the right categories.

If I could only fix one thing on most of the profiles I look at, it would be the primary category. It is the single biggest lever you have for local search ranking, and it is the one owners treat like a formality.

Here is what Google is doing under the hood: when someone types "Italian restaurant near me," Google filters the local map pack down to listings whose primary category is "Italian Restaurant." Listings with "Italian Restaurant" in their additional categories are candidates, but they rank below the primary-matches. So if you are an Italian place with "Restaurant" as your primary, you are losing to every other Italian spot in the neighborhood before the query even looks at your reviews or photos.

Primary category: pick the most specific one that applies. "Italian Restaurant" beats "Restaurant." "Brunch Restaurant" beats "American Restaurant" if brunch is your main draw. You get exactly one — make it count.

Additional categories: add 2–5 more that accurately describe your business. A restaurant that also does catering might add "Caterer." A place with a strong bar program might add "Bar" or "Cocktail Bar." Do not add categories you do not actually serve — Google suspends listings for misleading categories, and re-verification takes weeks.

I ran one of my restaurants on "Restaurant" as the primary category for the first two years we were open . That is me, somebody who does this for a living, sitting on a generic primary because nobody on staff thought to check. The day I switched it to the specific cuisine, our weekday rankings for "[cuisine] near me" moved up roughly five positions in the local pack. Not overnight — it took about a week. No other change, no new reviews, no new photos. Just the category.

If you do nothing else on this list, pull up your profile and look at your primary. If it says "Restaurant" and you are any kind of specific cuisine, that is thirty seconds to fix and real ranking in return.
Step 4 — Complete every field.
Most owners fill in name, address, phone, and hours — then stop. Here is what they miss:
Business description. You get 750 characters. Use them. Name your cuisine, your neighborhood, your sourcing philosophy, and your signature dishes. This is crawled by Google and shown to customers.

Menu link. Point this at your website's menu page, not a P D F. If you do not have a website yet, you can use Google's built-in menu editor — but a real web page is better for S E O and for the customer's reading experience.
Reservation link. If you use OpenTable, Resy, Tock, or any other platform, add the direct booking U R L here. Google will show a "Reserve a table" button on your listing.
Order link. Same idea — point to your direct ordering page (through Toast, Square, or your website), not to a third-party marketplace that charges you 30%.

Attributes. Google lets you specify: outdoor seating, wheelchair accessible, takes reservations, good for groups, good for kids, serves alcohol, live music, et cetera Check every attribute that applies. These filter into customer searches ("restaurants with outdoor seating near me").
Opening date. If your restaurant has been open since 1931 (like one of mine), put that date in. Heritage is a trust signal.
The restaurant on the next block is not beating you because their food is better. They are beating you because they filled in the attributes you left blank.
Step 5 — Add real photos.

Profiles with photos get meaningfully more clicks and direction-requests than profiles without. Google has said this publicly for years. What they do not say out loud is which photos actually move the needle. After shooting a few hundred of them for restaurants, I can tell you the ranking is roughly: the exterior with your sign clearly visible, the dining room at dinner service with people in it, one hero plate of your signature dish, a clear shot of your menu board, and then everything else. Stock photography is worse than nothing — Google seems to detect and down-rank obvious stock.
What to upload:
Cover photo: the single best shot of your food or your room. This is what appears in search results.
Logo: your restaurant's mark, square format, clean background.
Interior photos: the dining room, the bar, the patio. At least 3–5.
Food photos: your most photogenic dishes. Professional quality if possible — phone photos are fine if the lighting is good. At least 5–10.
Team photos: the chef, the bartender, the host stand. People trust faces.
Exterior photo: the storefront, clearly showing your sign. This helps customers find you on arrival.
Upload new photos at least once a month. Fresh photos signal an active business, and they give Google fresh content to surface.

At one of my places we used to batch-upload a dozen photos once a quarter when I had time. Then one month I tested a cadence of two photos a week — Monday morning, Thursday afternoon — for a season. Same restaurant, same quality of photos, just a slower drip. Map-pack impressions on weekday lunch queries roughly doubled over the quarter.

I cannot prove causation. But I have seen the pattern enough times now to believe Google treats consistent posting as a liveness signal more than it treats a big one-time dump as a content signal. Drip > dump.
Step 6 — Set up Google Posts.

Google Posts are short updates that appear directly on your listing — like social media for Google Maps. Most restaurants never use them, which means the ones that do stand out immediately. Use them for:
Weekly specials and seasonal menu changes
Events (live music, trivia night, holiday hours)
Promotions (happy hour, neighborhood discounts)
New menu items or seasonal drinks

Standard posts are archived after about six months (events expire after the event date). But freshness matters — Google surfaces recent posts more prominently than stale ones. Think of posting as a weekly habit, not a one-time setup. One post per week, published on Monday or Tuesday, keeps your listing active and signals to both Google and customers that the restaurant is alive.
Step 7 — Respond to every review.

I wrote an entire post about Google reviews , but the short version: respond to every review, positive and negative, within 24 hours. Keep responses short, specific, and human. Responding to reviews is both a customer service signal and a ranking signal — Google confirms this in their local ranking documentation.
The fifteen-minute weekly habit.
Once your profile is set up, maintenance is minimal. Here is the weekly routine:
Monday: publish one Google Post (this week's special, an event, or a fresh photo).
Daily (5 min): respond to any new reviews.
Monthly: upload 2–3 new photos. Update hours if they have changed. Check that your menu link still works.
Quarterly: review your attributes, update your description if your concept has evolved, and check your analytics to see which searches are finding you.
That is it. Fifteen minutes a week, plus a monthly check-in. The restaurants that do this consistently outrank the ones that set up their profile once and never touched it again.
